presentingComplaint: Progressive confusion, unsteadiness and double vision over 10 days in a frail, non-drinking elderly woman.
history: 79-year-old widow, lives alone, increasingly frail over the past year with 8 kg unintentional weight loss and poor appetite following her husband's death and a recent hip fracture. For the past 6 weeks she has eaten very little, subsisting mainly on tea and biscuits, with intermittent nausea and vomiting attributed to 'a bad tummy'. She was admitted 5 days ago for dehydration and a fall and started on IV 5% dextrose maintenance fluids without vitamin supplementation. Family now report she has become drowsy, muddled about where she is, apathetic, and has developed double vision and a staggering gait. No alcohol use (lifelong near-teetotaller). No fever, no headache, no focal weakness. Background: osteoporosis, mild cognitive baseline but independent until recently, hypertension.
examination: Cachectic, frail elderly woman. Disoriented to time and place, inattentive and apathetic (global confusional state) but no aphasia or hemiparesis. Eye movements: horizontal gaze-evoked nystagmus with impaired bilateral abduction (partial ophthalmoplegia). Gait wide-based and ataxic, unable to stand unaided; heel-shin dysmetria bilaterally. Reflexes reduced at ankles (peripheral neuropathy). No neck stiffness. No asterixis. No jaundice or stigmata of chronic liver disease.
imaging: MRI brain: symmetrical T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the mammillary bodies, medial thalami and periaqueductal grey matter, without diffusion restriction of a vascular territory; no acute infarct, no subdural collection, no mass lesion.
finalDiagnosis: Wernicke encephalopathy due to nutritional thiamine deficiency in a frail elderly woman, precipitated by carbohydrate (IV dextrose) loading without thiamine — a non-alcoholic presentation.
citations: EFNS — Guideline on diagnosis and management of Wernicke encephalopathy — 2010
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Thiamine (Vitamin B1) Deficiency and Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome
stewardship: Not applicable — non-infective diagnosis; no antimicrobial therapy indicated.
contraindications: Do NOT administer IV glucose/dextrose before parenteral thiamine — glucose loading can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy
Oral thiamine is inadequate for acute treatment (poor and unreliable enteral absorption); give parenteral (IV) thiamine
Correct coexisting hypomagnesaemia — magnesium is a cofactor and deficiency impairs thiamine-dependent enzyme activity and response to replacement
edgeCases: The classic triad (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia) is present in a minority; diagnosis is clinical and treatment must not await MRI or thiamine levels
Non-alcoholic causes (starvation, prolonged vomiting, hyperemesis, bariatric surgery, malignancy, refeeding) are frequently missed, especially in the elderly
Normal thiamine level does not exclude the diagnosis; empirical high-dose IV thiamine is low-risk and should be given on suspicion
expectedMaiK: Wernicke encephalopathy — a clinical emergency of thiamine deficiency presenting with confusion, ocular signs and gait ataxia; here in a non-alcoholic frail elderly woman with starvation and dextrose-precipitated decompensation.
expectedNextQuestions: Detailed dietary/nutritional history and duration of reduced intake or vomiting
Was IV dextrose or a carbohydrate load given before thiamine?
Any bariatric surgery, malignancy, hyperemesis or dialysis (non-alcoholic risk factors)?
Timeline and progression of ocular, gait and cognitive changes
expectedInvestigations: Immediate high-dose parenteral thiamine (do not delay for tests)
MRI brain (mammillary bodies, medial thalami, periaqueductal grey)
Serum magnesium, glucose, sodium, renal and liver function
Whole-blood thiamine / erythrocyte transketolase (result should not delay treatment)

investigations: Immediate high-dose IV thiamine before any glucose

regressionAssertions: Engine must rank wernicke as top diagnosis despite absence of alcohol history
Must flag contraindication: parenteral thiamine before IV glucose
Should recognise nutritional/starvation aetiology as a valid non-alcoholic cause
